OSINTdefender Despite publicly praising prior efforts and today’s successful detonation of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at a munitions plant in Middletown, Iowa by the U.S. Army. Privately, President Trump and other senior members of the administration are furious and demanding answers on who is to blame, sources familiar with the matter have told CBS News. White House officials have expressed frustration in internal conversations that they had to scramble to deal with the crisis, which rapidly became a national news story, with complaints from Iowa residents that they had not received sufficient notice about the potential dangers from detonation by the Army. The Army had known since spring that the lead azide posed a threat to the public and to the environment, having informed the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in March. But according to some officials, then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll failed to raise the issue to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or to other senior officials in the Trump Administration. However, another source familiar with the discussions surrounding the ammunition said the Army notified Hegseth’s office early on, but that the notification never directly reached Hegseth. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle learned of the stored chemicals and the risks in September, but didn't brief superiors, with discussions currently taking place about quietly moving Telle out of the acting role in coming weeks, several sources told CBS News. tweet
